descriptor.scene: The manager stays INSIDE his glowing machine and never sets foot on the porch. The camera is well back and the PORCH is the subject, in warm late-afternoon daylight. June sits in a wooden porch rocking chair at the centre-left of the frame, at full length and no taller than half the frame height, an open picture book held before her, reading aloud, her face soft and unhurried. Leaning at her knee, a small boy of about five SEEN FROM BEHIND ONLY: the back of his head and shoulders to us, his face never visible and never the subject. The open book is oriented for the two of them, tilted away from the camera, and there is no lettering and no readable text on its pages. Around them worn porch boards, a simple rail, a few green leaves, warm sun. At the FAR RIGHT EDGE of the frame, small, stands the glowing machine itself: a warm cream cabinet with one lit rectangular screen turned to face them, and INSIDE that lit screen, contained by it, the manager stands square and front-on at a hand-span tall, calm and attentive, mitten arms relaxed at his sides, watching quietly all the way through. He is inside the lit screen and bounded by its edges: never on the porch, never hovering in front of the glass, never a sticker or decal on the cabinet. His small plum glow is one warm dot at the frame's edge against the daylight. Composition: June and the boy centre-left, the machine small at the far right; the upper left stays calm warm sky and porch roof.
descriptor._caption: June changes one word, because the last five percent is always hers. Then Theo is on her lap on the porch, and the big doors in the book open easy, and the manager watches from the glowing machine the way managers do: quietly, and all the way through.
negatives: the boy's face visible, or the boy as the subject of the frame
the manager outside the screen, standing on the porch, hovering in front of the glass, or drawn as a sticker on the cabinet
eyeglasses on June, on her face, pushed up on her head or on a cord
June's hair worn down or cut short; it is a low silver bun at the nape
readable text or lettering on the book
a tablet, a flat slab or a frameless panel; the cabinet has a real lit rectangular screen
